quests.hint: Try stressing every word in "plenty of time" equally — it sounds stiff and unnatural, right? Which word loses its full vowel to fix that?
quests.explanation: English sentence rhythm relies on this kind of reduction — content words stay strong, function words like "of" go weak. That's why /ɒ/ becomes schwa in "plenty of time".
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Instead of hearing /d/ and /j/ separately between "send" and "your", listen for one fused sound. What is it?
quests.explanation: This is coalescent assimilation: two adjacent sounds merge into a third sound that resembles neither one alone. Here, /d/ and /j/ combine into /dʒ/ in "send your".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "isn't your" quickly and casually. The /t/ and the /j/ in "your" don't stay separate — what do they merge into?
quests.explanation: Rather than two separate consonants, connected speech blends /t/ and /j/ into /tʃ/. That's why "isn't your" sounds like one smooth unit rather than two words bumping together.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A bilabial consonant is coming up in "people". What does that do to the /n/ just before it in "ten"?
quests.explanation: Speakers save effort by letting /n/ anticipate the bilabial sound ahead. So in "ten people", /n/ is pronounced as /m/ instead.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "dinner is" naturally. That final 'r' in "dinner", usually silent, resurfaces here — why, do you think?
quests.explanation: This is linking, not intrusion, because the 'r' is already written into "dinner". It stays silent before a pause or consonant but comes back to life right before the vowel that opens "is".
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try saying "command line" at a natural conversational pace, not word by word. What happens to the /d/ sound in the middle?
quests.explanation: Native speakers rarely pronounce every consonant in a heavy cluster. In "command line", the /d/ is left out completely, letting the surrounding consonants connect directly.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Function words like "were" rarely keep their dictionary pronunciation in natural sentences. Listen for what its vowel becomes in "we were ready".
quests.explanation: Because "were" isn't emphasized in "we were ready", its vowel weakens from the full /ɜː/ to a fast, neutral schwa sound. This happens to almost every unstressed function word in fluent English.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
options: Gemination (the two /k/ sounds merge into one)
quests.correctAnswer: Gemination (the two /k/ sounds merge into one)

quests.explanation: This is a case of avoiding needless repetition — instead of two short /k/ sounds, English produces one held /k/ across "book" and "club", saving effort while staying clear.
quests.phoneticRule: Gemination avoids doubling identical adjacent consonants — the two collapse into one held sound rather than two short repetitions.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Both "comma" and "or" end and begin with vowel sounds. Listen for an extra consonant sound that sneaks in between them.
quests.explanation: This is intrusion: a sound appears between two vowels even though it isn't written anywhere. In "comma or", an intrusive /r/ bridges the gap, purely to avoid an awkward vowel collision.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Notice how the mouth has to move from the /n/ ending "seven" to the bilabial sound that opens "players". Does it really make that full move, or take a shortcut?
quests.explanation: Unlike elision, nothing is dropped here — the sound simply changes place. /n/ becomes /m/ in "seven players" to match the bilabial consonant that follows.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE

quests.explanation: Because "he" is unstressed, its /h/ disappears in natural speech, and the consonant ending "where's" links directly to the exposed vowel. That's why "where's he" sounds like one connected unit rather than two separate words.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak, unstressed pronouns like "him", "her", and "his" regularly lose their initial /h/ in fast, casual connected speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Three consonants in a row is hard work for the mouth. Focus on the /t/ where "just" meets "now" — does English keep it or drop it?
quests.explanation: Because /t/ is squeezed between two other consonants, it gets dropped in fluent speech. Say "just now" aloud and you'll notice the /t/ just isn't there.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
options: Linking (the consonant links to the vowel)
quests.hint: In "is he", "he" carries no stress. Unstressed h-words often lose that opening sound — does it happen here?
quests.explanation: H-dropping is extremely common with weak pronouns after a consonant. The /h/ in "he" vanishes, and "is"'s final sound carries straight over into the vowel left behind.
quests.phoneticRule: H-dropping removes the initial /h/ from unstressed pronouns and auxiliaries, letting the surrounding sounds link or glide together smoothly.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "speak up" as one smooth unit, not two separate words. Where does the final consonant of "speak" end up?
quests.explanation: This is linking: the consonant isn't added, dropped, or changed — it simply moves to attach to the following vowel. That's exactly what happens between "speak" and "up".
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.phoneticRule: When identical consonants meet at a word boundary, English merges them into a single, slightly longer sound instead of pronouncing both separately.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE

quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.phoneticRule: When identical consonants meet at a word boundary, English merges them into a single, slightly longer sound instead of pronouncing both separately.
